facts.statement: The eastern moa is the only species currently recognized within the genus Emeus.
facts.quote: It is the only species in the genus Emeus.

facts.statement: Richard Owen originally described the first specimens of this animal in 1846, initially placing them in the genus Dinornis.
facts.quote: When the first specimens were originally described by Richard Owen in 1846, they were placed within the genus Dinornis as three different species.

facts.statement: Remains originally classified as Dinornis were later reclassified into the distinct genus Emeus.
facts.quote: These remains would later be split off into their own genus, Emeus.

facts.statement: Researchers have long suspected that previously described species Emeus huttonii and E. crassus were actually male and female variants of a single species.
facts.quote: It has been long suspected that the "species" described as Emeus huttonii and E. crassus were males and females, respectively, of a single species.

facts.statement: Analysis of DNA from bone material confirmed that females of E. crassus were 15-25% larger than males.
facts.quote: This has been confirmed by analysis for sex-specific genetic markers of DNA extracted from bone material; the females of E. crassus were 15-25% larger than males.

facts.statement: The eastern moa stood approximately 1.5 meters tall and weighed between 36 and 79 kilograms.
facts.quote: Emeus was of average size, standing 1.5 to(-) tall, and weighing from 36 to 79kg.

facts.statement: The animal possessed a long neck, large powerful legs with short strong tarsi, and beige hair-like feathers without vestigial wing bones.
facts.quote: Like other moa, it had no vestigial wing bones, hair-like feathers (beige in this case), a long neck and large, powerful legs with very short, strong tarsi.

facts.statement: The tarsometatarsus of the eastern moa was restricted to motion in the parasagittal plane, similar to most other ratites.
facts.quote: Its tarsometatarsus was restricted in motion to the parasagittal plane, a condition much like that in most other ratites.

facts.statement: The pelvic musculature of the eastern moa was poorly adapted for running.
facts.quote: Emeus had pelvic musculature poorly adapted for cursoriality.

facts.statement: The eastern moa had exceptionally wide feet compared to other moa species, making it a very slow creature.
facts.quote: Its feet were exceptionally wide compared to other moas, making it a very slow creature.

facts.statement: The eggs of the eastern moa measured 17.9 by 13.4 centimeters and weighed 1.9 kilograms.
facts.quote: Eggs were 17.9 / 13.4 cm, and weighed 1.9 kg.

facts.statement: The eastern moa lived exclusively on the South Island of New Zealand, inhabiting lowland forests, grasslands, dunelands, and shrublands.
facts.quote: Eastern moa lived only on the South Island of New Zealand, inhabiting lowland habitats like forests, grasslands, dunelands, and shrublands.

facts.statement: During the Last Glacial Maximum, the eastern moa was confined to a single glacial refugium before its range expanded during the Holocene.
facts.quote: During the Last Glacial Maximum, it was confined to a single glacial refugium, from which its range expanded during the Holocene.

facts.statement: The eastern moa species went extinct around the year 1400.
facts.quote: The species had gone extinct around the year 1400.

facts.statement: The eastern moa is classified in the class Aves, order Dinornithiformes, and family Dinornithidae.
